sections.heading: What the California Clean Truck Check program asks of you
sections.body:
The California Clean Truck Check program requires most diesel and alternative-fuel vehicles over 14,000 lb GVWR to report to CARB and pass periodic emissions tests. Its formal name is the Heavy-Duty Inspection and Maintenance program. You may see it called the HD I/M program in California, or CARB HD I/M, but most drivers just call it Clean Truck Check.

For an owner, CARB Clean Truck Check comes down to three jobs:

1. Report each vehicle in CARB's CTC-VIS system and pay the annual compliance fee shown there.
2. Pass each Clean Truck Check test by your deadline. Most covered vehicles currently test twice a year.
3. If a truck fails, get it repaired and pass a retest.

The rules cover California-registered trucks and also out-of-state and international trucks that operate in California. Buses, refuse trucks, construction and agricultural vehicles and motorhomes over 14,000 lb can be included too, so check CARB's rules for your vehicle if you are unsure.

The [Clean Truck Check requirements page](/clean-truck-check) walks through each step in more detail, and our [FAQ](/clean-truck-check/faq) answers the do-I-need-it questions.

sections.heading: Truck smog check or Clean Truck Check? Same need, different program
sections.body:
If you are searching for a truck smog check in California, the test you most likely need is Clean Truck Check. Drivers still say semi truck smog check, big rig smog check or heavy duty smog check, but for vehicles over 14,000 lb GVWR the emissions testing is run by CARB under Clean Truck Check.

Which test your truck gets depends on the engine:

- **2013 and newer diesel** and **2018 and newer alternative-fuel** engines get a CARB-verified [OBD test](/services/obd-testing).
- **2012 and older diesel** without OBD gets a [smoke opacity test](/services/smoke-opacity-test) plus a visual inspection.
- **2017 and older alternative-fuel** without OBD gets a visual inspection.

So a diesel truck smog check in California, or a semi truck smog check in California, for a newer tractor usually means plugging in to read the engine's own emissions data, while an older dump truck gets a smoke test. Either way, it is a commercial truck smog test with its own rules and its own reporting in CTC-VIS. For a side-by-side look, read [Clean Truck Check vs. smog check](/blog/clean-truck-check-vs-smog-check).

sections.heading: Keeping up with California truck emissions compliance
sections.body:
California truck emissions compliance is ongoing, not a one-time box to check. Each covered vehicle has a deadline in CTC-VIS, a yearly compliance fee owed to CARB, and a test to pass on schedule.

Missing it has real costs. California-registered vehicles can get a DMV registration hold, and CARB can issue citations and penalties to trucks that operate in the state without being compliant.

sections.heading: The Clean Truck Check regulation in one paragraph
sections.body:
Clean Truck Check is the public name for CARB's heavy duty inspection and maintenance regulation, often called the HD I/M regulation. The California Clean Truck Check law covers most diesel and alternative-fuel vehicles over 14,000 lb GVWR that operate in the state, whether they are registered in California, another state or another country.

The idea is simple. Trucks are built with emissions controls, and this regulation checks that those controls still work out on the road. That is why the test looks at the engine's OBD data on newer trucks, and at smoke and visible equipment on older ones.

Clean Truck Check covers tractor trailers, but it also covers much more. Box trucks, dump trucks, buses, refuse trucks, construction and agricultural vehicles and motorhomes over 14,000 lb can all be part of the CARB heavy duty vehicle inspection program. Edge cases exist, so check CARB's rules for your vehicle.

If you want to know why the state does this at all, read [why California enforces it](/clean-truck-check/why-california-enforces-it).

sections.heading: When is my Clean Truck Check due? Finding your deadline
sections.body:
Your Clean Truck Check deadline is listed for each vehicle in CARB's CTC-VIS system. That is the one place for a Clean Truck Check deadline lookup, because deadlines are set per vehicle rather than one date for everyone.

A few practical tips:

- **Log in to CTC-VIS and check each VIN.** If a vehicle is missing, it needs to be added before it can show as compliant. Our [CTC-VIS registration guide](/blog/ctc-vis-registration-guide) walks through it.
- **Book ahead of the date, not on it.** A failed test means repair and a retest, and that takes time.
- **Keep a calendar for every truck.** With most vehicles testing twice a year, a small fleet quickly has a lot of dates.

When we test your truck, we give you the next due date and can send a reminder before it arrives. Fleets can set up recurring visits so nobody has to track the dates by hand.

If a date has already passed, act quickly. See [what to do after a missed Clean Truck Check deadline](/blog/missed-clean-truck-check-deadline).

sections.heading: Clean Truck Check compliance fee vs. the testing fee
sections.body:
There are two separate costs in Clean Truck Check: CARB's annual compliance fee and the testing fee. They go to different places and are paid in different ways.

- **The compliance fee** is set by CARB and charged per vehicle each year. You pay it in CTC-VIS, where the current amount is shown. It is the same no matter which tester you use.
- **The testing fee** is what the tester charges to perform the test. Ours depends on how many trucks we test, the test type and your location, with per-truck pricing for fleets.

Paying one does not cover the other. A truck can pass its test and still not be compliant if the annual fee is unpaid, and paying the fee does not replace the test.

We do not collect CARB's fee, but we are happy to point you to the right screen in CTC-VIS. For more detail, see [the compliance fee explained](/blog/clean-truck-check-compliance-fee-explained) and [how much Clean Truck Check costs](/blog/how-much-does-clean-truck-check-cost-california). For a testing quote, call or text (858) 342-8328.

sections.heading: Clean Truck Check exemptions: check before you assume
sections.body:
Some vehicles fall outside Clean Truck Check or follow special rules, but the details are set by CARB and they matter. Do not assume a vehicle belongs on the list of Clean Truck Check exempt vehicles, and do not assume a truck is exempt because it is new, used rarely or owned by a farm or public agency.

The safest path is:

1. Confirm the GVWR. The program is aimed at vehicles over 14,000 lb.
2. Confirm the fuel. It covers diesel and alternative-fuel engines.
3. Check CARB's rules for your vehicle, or ask CARB directly, if you think an exemption applies.

Guessing wrong is costly. A California-registered vehicle that should have tested can end up with a DMV registration hold, and CARB can issue citations and penalties.

We can tell you which test a covered truck needs from the engine model year or VIN, and we will say plainly when a question belongs with CARB. Our post on [Clean Truck Check exemptions](/blog/clean-truck-check-exemptions) and the guide to [which vehicles need Clean Truck Check](/blog/which-vehicles-need-clean-truck-check) go deeper.

sections.heading: Where Clean Truck Check fits in California truck emissions regulations
sections.body:
Clean Truck Check is the part of California truck emissions regulations that checks whether a truck's emissions controls still work. Other CARB heavy duty emissions rules, such as the Truck and Bus Regulation, deal with which engines may operate. Clean Truck Check asks a different question: is this truck's equipment doing its job today?

That is why Clean Truck Check exists. A clean engine when new can become a dirty one after a fault, a clogged filter or a removed part. Periodic testing catches those problems:

- **Newer trucks** get an OBD test that reads the engine's own emissions data.
- **Older diesel trucks** without OBD get a smoke opacity test and a visual inspection.
- **Older alternative-fuel trucks** without OBD get a visual inspection.

For drivers, the practical takeaway is that California diesel emissions laws for trucks, and California trucking emissions requirements in general, are not only about buying the right truck. They are about keeping it in working order. A truck with a check engine light, unset readiness monitors, DPF faults or deleted equipment will not pass. For the full list of rules you need to follow, see the [Clean Truck Check requirements](/clean-truck-check).

sections.heading: Why Southern California is a focus for truck pollution
sections.body:
Truck pollution in Southern California gets extra attention because heavy trucks are everywhere here. The Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach move freight day and night. Drayage trucks carry it to rail yards and to warehouses across the Inland Empire. From there, trucks fan out to Orange County, San Diego and the Imperial Valley border crossings.

That means many people live and work close to busy truck routes, ports and distribution centers. When a truck's emissions system is not working, the effect is felt right where those trucks idle, load and travel.

Port of LA truck pollution regulations and Inland Empire warehouse truck emissions rules both include this same test. Clean Truck Check applies statewide, so the same rules cover a port drayage tractor, an Inland Empire warehouse truck and a San Diego delivery fleet. The test does not change by county.

We test in all of these places. Our mobile testers go to [port terminals](/service-areas/ports/port-of-los-angeles), [Inland Empire](/service-areas/inland-empire) yards and jobsites across the region, so staying compliant does not mean pulling a truck off its route to find a test site.

sections.heading: Who enforces Clean Truck Check
sections.body:
CARB runs and enforces Clean Truck Check, and the California DMV plays a role for California-registered vehicles. Here is how enforcement shows up for truck owners:

- **DMV registration holds.** A California-registered vehicle that is out of compliance can be blocked from renewing its registration until the problem is fixed.
- **CARB citations and penalties.** Trucks that operate in California without meeting the rules can be cited, and this includes out-of-state and international trucks.
- **CTC-VIS records.** Compliance is tracked per vehicle in CARB's CTC-VIS system, which is where reporting, fees and test results come together.

Diesel Dynamix is not part of that enforcement. We are an independent testing service, not CARB or a government agency. Our job is to test your trucks on site, explain the results in plain English and help you stay ahead of each deadline.

If a vehicle already has a hold, read our guide to [Clean Truck Check DMV registration holds](/blog/dmv-registration-hold-clean-truck-check).

sections.heading: California heavy duty truck regulations: 2026 and beyond
sections.body:
For 2026, the main Clean Truck Check rule for most covered vehicles is testing twice a year, along with reporting in CTC-VIS and paying CARB's annual compliance fee. What comes next is less settled.

Under CARB's original rule, OBD-equipped vehicles move to four tests per year starting October 1, 2027. A bill has also proposed cutting testing to once a year. Until the rule is final, plan for the schedule CARB has in place and check your deadlines in CTC-VIS.

What this means in practice:

- **Owner-operators** should keep each due date on the calendar and book before it, not on it.
- **Fleets** should plan for more test visits if the 2027 change goes ahead.
- **Everyone** should fix check engine lights and emissions faults early, since a failing truck needs repair and a retest.

We follow these changes so you do not have to. We give you the next due date after every test and can set up recurring [fleet visits](/services/fleet-testing). Our [2026-2027 deadlines post](/blog/clean-truck-check-2026-2027-deadlines) has the latest.

faqs.q: Why does California test truck emissions?
faqs.a: California tests heavy truck emissions to make sure each truck's emissions controls still work on the road. Clean Truck Check catches faults, failing parts and tampered equipment that would otherwise add pollution.

faqs.q: Who enforces Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: CARB enforces Clean Truck Check with citations and penalties, and the California DMV can place registration holds on California-registered vehicles that are not compliant.

faqs.q: Is Clean Truck Check the same as the CARB Truck and Bus Regulation?
faqs.a: No. The CARB Truck and Bus Regulation, often called the truck and bus rule, is a separate California rule. Clean Truck Check is the periodic testing program that checks whether a truck's emissions controls are working.

faqs.q: Do Inland Empire warehouse trucks follow different emissions rules?
faqs.a: Clean Truck Check is statewide, so a truck serving Inland Empire warehouses follows the same testing rules as any other covered vehicle operating in California.

faqs.q: What are the CARB truck regulations for 2026?
faqs.a: In 2026, most vehicles covered by Clean Truck Check test twice a year, report in CTC-VIS and pay CARB's annual compliance fee. Four tests per year for OBD-equipped vehicles is scheduled from October 1, 2027 under CARB's original rule.

faqs.q: Is Clean Truck Check mandatory?
faqs.a: Yes, for covered vehicles. Most diesel and alternative-fuel vehicles over 14,000 lb GVWR that operate in California must report in CTC-VIS, pay CARB's annual fee and pass periodic tests.

faqs.q: How do I know if my truck needs Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: Check the GVWR and fuel type. If it is over 14,000 lb GVWR, runs on diesel or an alternative fuel and operates in California, it most likely needs Clean Truck Check; check CARB's rules for edge cases.

faqs.q: Do pickup trucks need Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: Only if the pickup is over 14,000 lb GVWR and runs on diesel or an alternative fuel. Most everyday pickups are under that weight, but check the GVWR rating for your truck.

faqs.q: Do I need a smog check for my diesel truck in California?
faqs.a: If your diesel truck is over 14,000 lb GVWR, the emissions test you need is CARB's Clean Truck Check. A 2013 or newer engine gets an OBD test, and a 2012 or older engine without OBD gets a smoke opacity test and visual inspection.

faqs.q: Do semi trucks need smog check in California?
faqs.a: Yes. Semi trucks over 14,000 lb GVWR that operate in California need Clean Truck Check testing, including out-of-state and international trucks.

faqs.q: Do box trucks need smog check in California?
faqs.a: Box trucks over 14,000 lb GVWR that run on diesel or an alternative fuel need Clean Truck Check. Lighter box trucks are below the program's weight threshold.

faqs.q: Do dump trucks need smog check?
faqs.a: Yes, dump trucks over 14,000 lb GVWR that operate in California need Clean Truck Check. Older diesel dump trucks without OBD get a smoke opacity test and visual inspection.

faqs.q: Do motorhomes need smog check in California?
faqs.a: Diesel and alternative-fuel motorhomes over 14,000 lb GVWR can fall under Clean Truck Check. Check CARB's rules for your specific motorhome, and see our motorhome guide for details.

faqs.q: Is Clean Truck Check the same as smog check?
faqs.a: Not exactly. Many people call it a truck smog check, but Clean Truck Check is CARB's program for heavy vehicles over 14,000 lb GVWR, with its own tests and reporting in CTC-VIS.

faqs.q: What year trucks need Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: Covered trucks of any model year need Clean Truck Check; the year decides the test. Newer engines get an OBD test, while older diesel engines without OBD get a smoke opacity test and visual inspection.

faqs.q: Can I do Clean Truck Check myself or buy my own OBD device?
faqs.a: Not with a regular scan tool, so a DIY Clean Truck Check is not an option. Clean Truck Check tests must be done by a credentialed tester using CARB-verified equipment, so check CARB's rules if you want to test your own trucks.

faqs.q: Does Clean Truck Check apply to trailers?
faqs.a: The test is done on the engine-powered vehicle, such as the tractor pulling the trailer. A trailer with no engine has nothing to test, but check CARB's rules for unusual equipment.

faqs.q: Is there a grace period for Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: Do not count on one. Missing your deadline can lead to a DMV registration hold for California-registered vehicles and CARB citations and penalties, so test before the date shown in CTC-VIS.

faqs.a: Testing fees are set by each tester. Our price depends on the number of trucks, the test type and your location, and we test single trucks as well as fleets; call or text (858) 342-8328 for a quote.

sections.heading: What the CARB OBD test checks on your truck
sections.body:
The CARB OBD test reads the emissions data your truck's on-board computer already keeps and records it for the Clean Truck Check program. It is the required test for 2013 and newer diesel engines and 2018 and newer alternative-fuel engines.

Our tester plugs CARB-verified equipment into the diagnostic port. Nobody drives the truck. In plain terms, the scan looks at:

- Whether the check engine light (MIL) is on
- Stored emissions-related fault codes
- Whether the readiness monitors have run and are set

Those same items cause most failures. The usual reasons a truck does not pass are a lit check engine light, readiness monitors that are not set (often after a battery disconnect or cleared codes), DPF and other emissions faults, and tampered or deleted equipment. Deleted systems fail and are illegal, and we do not help with them.

So the Clean Truck Check OBD pass requirements come down to a working emissions system with no open faults. If something is off, we explain the result in plain English so your shop knows what to fix before the retest. More detail: [check engine light and readiness monitors](/blog/readiness-monitors-check-engine-light-clean-truck-check).

We test them all on site, including:

- **Freightliner** Cascadia and M2
- **Peterbilt** 579 and 389
- **Kenworth** T680 and T880
- **International** LT and ProStar
- **Volvo** VNL
- **Mack** Anthem and Granite

Day cab or sleeper, the process is the same: connect, read, record, explain. The brand matters far less than the condition of the emissions system. A Freightliner OBD test and a Peterbilt OBD test fail for the same reasons, such as an active check engine light or monitors that have not finished their drive cycle.

Medium-duty trucks follow the same rule. An OBD emissions test for a box truck works the same way when the vehicle is over 14,000 lb GVWR and falls under the program.

For brand-specific tips on readiness monitors and port locations, see [OBD test by truck brand](/blog/obd-test-by-truck-brand).

Propane trucks, hybrid trucks and gasoline trucks over 14,000 lb GVWR can also fall under Clean Truck Check. These are the edge cases where details matter, so check CARB's rules for your vehicle before you book. If you are not sure what applies, call us. sections.heading: What a smoke opacity test measures
sections.body:
A smoke opacity test measures how much smoke a diesel engine puts out when it is revved hard from idle. California uses it, along with a visual inspection, as the Clean Truck Check test for 2012 and older diesel engines without OBD.

Here is how the smoke opacity test is done. With the engine at normal operating temperature, our tester fits an opacity meter to the exhaust. The engine is then taken through a series of snap accelerations: quick full-throttle revs from idle, which is why some drivers call it a snap idle test. The meter reads the smoke from each snap, and the readings are combined into one result.

California smoke opacity limits are set by CARB and depend on the engine's model year, so two trucks with the same reading can get different results. We do not guess. After the test we tell you the reading, whether the truck passed and, if it did not, what usually causes that much smoke.

Want to improve your odds before test day? Read [how to pass the CARB smoke test](/blog/how-to-pass-carb-smoke-test).

sections.heading: The visual inspection: labels, parts and tampering
sections.body:
Every diesel smoke test comes with a CARB visual inspection, and a truck has to pass both. A clean smoke reading does not save a truck that fails the visual check.

During the emissions visual inspection, our tester looks at:

- The emission control label (ECL) on the engine
- The emissions-control parts the engine should have
- Signs that parts are missing, disconnected, modified or tampered with

A tamper inspection on a diesel truck in California is strict. Deleted or tampered emissions equipment fails, and running it is illegal. We will not help with deletes. If a part is missing, the fix is to put the right part back and retest.

Older alternative-fuel trucks are a different case. A 2017 or older alternative-fuel engine without OBD does not take an opacity test at all. It gets the visual inspection only. Newer alternative-fuel engines use the [CARB OBD test](/services/obd-testing).

sections.heading: Smoke test for older diesel trucks, dump trucks and motorhomes

A lot of older equipment still works hard in Southern California and falls in this group:

- Dump trucks and water trucks on construction jobs
- Agricultural and farm trucks
- Older tractors with engines such as the Detroit Series 60, Cummins N14 or Caterpillar C15
- Refuse, tow and utility trucks from before 2013
- Diesel motorhomes over 14,000 lb GVWR, where they fall under the program

Engine make does not change the test. A Detroit Series 60 smoke test and a Cummins N14 opacity test follow the same steps. What changes the result is condition: injectors, turbo, air intake, exhaust leaks and any particulate filter.

Not sure if your vehicle is covered? Check CARB's rules for your vehicle, especially for motorhomes and specialty equipment, or call us with the engine details.

pages.title: How Does Clean Truck Check Work? The Test Process

sections.heading: How does Clean Truck Check work, start to finish?
sections.body:
Clean Truck Check works in three parts: the owner reports the vehicle in CARB's CTC-VIS system, pays CARB's annual compliance fee, and has the truck pass the right emissions test before each deadline. Diesel Dynamix handles the testing part, on site.

Here are the Clean Truck Check test steps with a mobile tester:

1. **Report and pay.** Make sure each truck is in CTC-VIS and the annual fee is paid. We can help if you are stuck.
2. **Check the deadline.** Each truck has its own due dates in CTC-VIS.
3. **Book the visit.** Tell us the truck count, engine types and where the trucks park.
4. **Test day.** We run the right test for each truck: OBD for 2013+ diesel and 2018+ alternative fuel, smoke opacity plus visual inspection for 2012 and older diesel without OBD, or visual inspection for 2017 and older alternative fuel without OBD.
5. **Results.** You get the result per truck, a plain-English explanation and the next due date.

If a truck fails, it goes to a repair shop, then we retest. We do not do repairs.

sections.heading: Clean Truck Check checklist: how to prepare
sections.body:
Most problems on test day are preventable. Use this checklist in the days before the visit.

**Paperwork and access**

- The VIN for every truck. Each test is tied to the VIN, so it has to match the truck.
- Your CTC-VIS login, or at least confirmation that each truck is reported and the fee is paid.
- Keys, cab access and gate instructions for our tester.

**Truck condition**

- No check engine light. Get faults diagnosed and repaired before the test, not the morning of.
- Do not clear codes or disconnect the battery right before an OBD test. The readiness monitors need time and driving to set again.
- For smoke tests, fix known smoke problems such as a dirty air filter, exhaust leaks or a failing injector.
- Any particulate filter should be installed and working. Deleted or tampered equipment fails.

**Scheduling**

- Group trucks with close deadlines into one visit.
- Ask for an early-morning slot if trucks need to roll out on time.

sections.heading: What happens during a mobile Clean Truck Check test
sections.body:
On test day, our tester arrives at your location, checks in with your contact and works through the trucks one at a time. You do not drive anywhere.

For an OBD truck, the tester confirms the VIN, connects CARB-verified equipment to the diagnostic port and records the data. The truck stays parked. For a non-OBD diesel, the engine is brought to operating temperature, the tester does the visual inspection, and the opacity meter reads the smoke during several snap accelerations. Older alternative-fuel trucks without OBD get the visual inspection.

How long Clean Truck Check takes depends on the mix. OBD tests are usually quick once connected. Smoke tests take longer because of warm-up and the inspection. A large yard takes longer than a single truck, which is why we plan the order around your dispatch.

As each truck finishes, we tell you how it did. If one fails, we explain why in plain English, so your mechanic knows where to start, and we schedule the retest after the repair.

sections.heading: Proof of compliance and how long a test lasts
sections.body:
A passing test counts toward the truck's current deadline, and the truck's compliance status is tracked in CARB's CTC-VIS system. That status, along with your test records, is your Clean Truck Check proof of compliance.

To stay compliant, three things have to be true: the truck is reported in CTC-VIS, CARB's annual fee is paid, and the truck has passed its test for the current period. If any one is missing, the truck can show as non-compliant even after a passing test.

A test is not good forever. Most covered vehicles currently test twice a year. Under CARB's original rule, OBD-equipped vehicles move to four tests a year from October 1, 2027. A bill has proposed cutting testing to once a year, so the schedule may change. Always check each truck's next due date in CTC-VIS.

We keep a record for every truck by VIN, give you the next due date and can send reminders before it comes up. Fleets can set up recurring visits. See [fleet testing](/services/fleet-testing).

faqs.q: How long does Clean Truck Check take for one truck?
faqs.a: An OBD test is usually quick once the tester is connected, because the truck does not need to be driven. A smoke opacity test takes longer because the engine must be warmed up and a visual inspection is done.

faqs.q: Does the truck need to be warmed up for the smoke test?
faqs.a: Yes. The engine should reach normal operating temperature before a smoke opacity test, because a cold engine smokes more. OBD tests do not need a warm-up drive.

faqs.q: What documents are needed for Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: Have the VIN for each truck and confirmation that each truck is reported in CTC-VIS with CARB's annual fee paid. The tester also needs keys and cab access.

faqs.q: How do I get proof of Clean Truck Check compliance?
faqs.a: Report the truck in CTC-VIS, pay CARB's annual fee and pass the required test before the deadline. The truck's status in CTC-VIS shows compliance, and Diesel Dynamix gives you a test record for each VIN.

faqs.q: Do I need to be present for a mobile truck emissions test?
faqs.a: You do not have to stand by the truck, but our tester needs keys, cab access and a contact on site or by phone. Many customers leave the keys with a yard manager.

faqs.q: How long is a Clean Truck Check test valid?
faqs.a: A passing test covers the truck until its next deadline. Most covered vehicles test twice a year today, and under the original rule OBD trucks move to four tests a year from October 1, 2027.

faqs.q: How soon do I get my Clean Truck Check test results?
faqs.a: Diesel Dynamix tells you how each truck did right after its test on site. If a truck fails, we explain the reason in plain English and plan the retest.

CARB sets the official recordkeeping rules, so check CARB's rules for your fleet type.

pages.title: Clean Truck Check Basics for California Truck Owners
pages.description: Clean Truck Check basics in plain English: which trucks are covered, which test yours needs, what CTC-VIS is and what happens if you fall behind.

sections.heading: Clean Truck Check terms in plain English
sections.body:
New to the program? These are the words you will see most.

- **Clean Truck Check (CTC):** CARB's emissions testing program for most diesel and alternative-fuel vehicles over 14,000 lb GVWR that operate in California. Many drivers just call it a truck smog check.
- **CARB:** the California Air Resources Board, which runs the program and sets the rules, fees and deadlines.
- **CTC-VIS:** CARB's online system where owners report each vehicle, pay the annual compliance fee and check deadlines.
- **GVWR:** gross vehicle weight rating, the maximum loaded weight the truck is rated for. Over 14,000 lb is the line for most of the program.
- **OBD test:** the test for 2013 and newer diesel and 2018 and newer alternative-fuel engines. See [OBD testing](/services/obd-testing).
- **Smoke opacity test:** the test, with a visual inspection, for 2012 and older diesel without OBD. See [smoke opacity testing](/services/smoke-opacity-test).
- **Non-compliant:** a truck that missed a step. California-registered trucks can get a DMV registration hold, and CARB can issue citations and penalties.

Diesel Dynamix is an independent testing service, not CARB.

sections.heading: Three things every truck owner has to do
sections.body:
Staying compliant comes down to three steps, repeated on schedule.

1. **Report the truck in CTC-VIS.** Every covered vehicle that operates in California has to be in the system, including out-of-state and international trucks.
2. **Pay CARB's annual compliance fee.** The amount is set by CARB and shown in CTC-VIS. It is separate from the testing fee a tester charges.
3. **Pass the test before each deadline.** Most covered vehicles currently test twice a year. Under CARB's original rule, OBD trucks move to four tests a year from October 1, 2027, and a bill has proposed once a year, so check CTC-VIS for your dates.

If a truck fails, it needs a repair and a retest. The usual causes are a check engine light, readiness monitors not set, DPF or emissions faults, or tampered equipment.

The easiest way to stay ahead is a tester who comes to you, gives you the next due date and reminds you before it arrives. [Book a test](/book) or call **(858) 342-8328**.

faqs.q: Who runs the Clean Truck Check program?
faqs.a: The California Air Resources Board (CARB) runs Clean Truck Check and sets its rules, fees and deadlines. Testing is done by testers such as Diesel Dynamix, an independent company that is not part of CARB.

faqs.q: Why do drivers call Clean Truck Check a truck smog check?
faqs.a: Truck smog check is the everyday name many drivers use, but Clean Truck Check is CARB's own program for most diesel and alternative-fuel vehicles over 14,000 lb GVWR. It uses an OBD test, a smoke opacity test or a visual inspection depending on the engine.

faqs.q: What does GVWR over 14,000 lb mean for Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: GVWR is the maximum loaded weight a vehicle is rated for. Most diesel and alternative-fuel vehicles rated over 14,000 lb that operate in California are covered by Clean Truck Check.

faqs.q: Are buses and motorhomes part of Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: Buses and motorhomes over 14,000 lb GVWR can fall under the program, along with refuse, construction and agricultural vehicles. Check CARB's rules for your vehicle to confirm.

pages.title: How Often Do Trucks Need Clean Truck Check? 2026-2027
pages.description: How often do trucks need Clean Truck Check? Twice a year for most trucks now, four times a year for OBD trucks from October 2027 under the original rule.

sections.heading: Clean Truck Check frequency in 2026 and 2027
sections.body:
Most covered trucks test twice a year in 2026. Under CARB's original rule, that changes for OBD-equipped trucks on October 1, 2027.

**Now (2026):**

- Most covered vehicles: two tests a year, which works out to roughly one every six months.
- This applies to OBD trucks and to older diesels that take the smoke opacity test.

**From October 1, 2027 (original rule):**

- OBD-equipped vehicles: four tests a year.
- The quarterly change applies to OBD trucks. Non-OBD trucks that take the smoke opacity test are not part of that change under the original rule.

**What could change:** a bill has proposed cutting Clean Truck Check to once a year. Until a change is final, plan for the current schedule.

How often semi trucks need emissions testing in California is the same answer as any other covered truck: it depends on the engine type and CARB's current rule. Your own due dates are always in CTC-VIS.

sections.heading: Building a Clean Truck Check schedule by truck
sections.body:
Each truck has its own due dates, so the schedule has to be by truck, not by fleet. Two trucks in the same yard can be due months apart.

A simple way to set it up:

1. Pull every truck's deadline from CTC-VIS.
2. Make one list by VIN with the test type (OBD or smoke) and next due date.
3. Group trucks with nearby deadlines so one visit covers several.
4. Leave time for a retest in case a truck fails and needs a repair.

When quarterly testing starts for OBD trucks, the same list keeps working. It just has more dates on it.

Diesel Dynamix does this tracking for you. After each test we give you the truck's next due date, keep the record by VIN, send reminders and can set up recurring visits to your yard. See [fleet testing](/services/fleet-testing) or call **(858) 342-8328**.

faqs.q: How many times a year is Clean Truck Check required?
faqs.a: Most covered vehicles currently test twice a year. Under CARB's original rule, OBD-equipped vehicles move to four tests a year starting October 1, 2027.

faqs.q: Is Clean Truck Check every 6 months?
faqs.a: Twice a year works out to roughly every six months, but each truck has its own due dates. Check the exact dates in CARB's CTC-VIS system.

faqs.q: Will Clean Truck Check go to once a year?
faqs.a: A bill has proposed cutting Clean Truck Check testing to once a year, so the schedule may change. Until a change is final, plan for the current twice-a-year schedule.

faqs.q: Will trucks need Clean Truck Check 4 times a year in 2027?
faqs.a: Under CARB's original rule, OBD-equipped vehicles move to four tests a year starting October 1, 2027. Non-OBD trucks are not part of that change under the original rule.

faqs.q: How often is a smoke opacity test required in California?
faqs.a: Older diesels that take the smoke opacity test currently test twice a year, like most covered vehicles. Check each truck's due dates in CTC-VIS.

faqs.q: When are my two Clean Truck Check tests due each year?
faqs.a: Due dates are set per truck and listed in CARB's CTC-VIS system. Diesel Dynamix gives you the next due date after each test and can send reminders.

sections.heading: Arizona, Texas, Mexico or Canada: the same rules apply
sections.body:
Where a truck is registered does not change Clean Truck Check. A covered truck from Arizona, Nevada, Texas, Mexico or Canada follows the same rules as a California truck once it operates in California.

That includes:

- **Interstate carriers** with trucks that run in and out of California
- **IRP trucks** on apportioned plates
- **Mexico-registered trucks** that cross the border into California
- **Canadian trucks** on California runs

Every one of these trucks needs to be reported in CTC-VIS, have CARB's annual compliance fee paid and pass the right test before its deadline. Out-of-state truck CTC-VIS registration works the same as for a California truck, and each truck's deadline is listed there.

The consequences differ a little. The DMV registration hold applies to California-registered vehicles. A non-California registered truck will not get a California DMV hold, but it can still face CARB citations and penalties if it operates while non-compliant.

If you are unsure whether your truck is covered, check CARB's rules for your vehicle or call us with your CTC-VIS questions.

sections.heading: Clean Truck Check cost vs the cost of falling behind
sections.body:
The cheapest Clean Truck Check is the one you do on time. A test costs money, but a non-compliant truck can cost more.

Here is what is at stake when a truck misses its deadline:

- **DMV registration hold** for California-registered trucks, which can stop the truck from being renewed.
- **CARB citations and penalties.** Amounts are set by CARB.
- **Lost work.** A truck that cannot run legally does not earn, and some customers and ports check compliance status.

Testing on site also cuts the hidden costs. A driver taking a truck to a test site loses fuel and hours, and the truck is off the road. With mobile testing, the truck is tested where it parks and goes back to work.

A failed test adds a repair and a retest, so keeping check engine lights and emissions faults fixed between tests saves money too. The common causes are a lit check engine light, readiness monitors not set, DPF or emissions faults, and tampered or deleted equipment.

pages.title: How to Pass the CARB Smoke Test on an Older Diesel
pages.description: How to pass the CARB smoke test: what to fix before test day, what to do after a snap test fail, and whether additives or a hard run help.

sections.heading: Failed the snap test? How to fix it
sections.body:
A failed snap test means the engine made too much smoke for its model year, or the truck failed the visual inspection. The fix is a repair, then a retest.

Start with what the result tells you:

- **High smoke reading.** Have a mechanic check the usual suspects: injectors, turbocharger, air filter and intake, exhaust leaks, and the particulate filter if the truck has one.
- **Visual inspection fail.** A missing, disconnected or tampered emissions part fails the truck even with a good smoke reading. The part has to be put back or repaired.
- **Deleted equipment.** Deleted or tampered systems fail and are illegal. The only path is to restore the equipment.

We do not do repairs, but we explain the result in plain English so your shop knows where to start. Bring the repair records to the retest if you have them.

Plan for this before the deadline. If an older truck is borderline, test early so there is time to fix it and retest. More on causes of smoke: [DPF, deletes and smoke](/blog/dpf-deletes-and-smoke-clean-truck-check).

sections.heading: Fuel additives and a hard run: do they help?
sections.body:
They are not a fix. An older diesel passes the opacity test because its engine and emissions parts are in good shape, not because of a bottle or a trick.

**Fuel additives.** We cannot tell you that any additive will get a truck through a smoke test. If the injectors are worn or the turbo is failing, an additive does not repair them.

**The "Italian tune-up."** A good hard run before the test does one useful thing: it gets the engine fully warm, and a cold engine smokes more. That is the same reason we ask for the truck at operating temperature. It will not fix worn parts.

What does help an older diesel pass:

- A full warm-up before the test
- Repairs done ahead of time, not the morning of
- A clean air filter and no exhaust leaks
- A working, intact particulate filter if the truck has one
- All original emissions parts in place for the visual inspection

faqs.q: Do fuel additives help a diesel pass the smoke test?
faqs.a: An additive does not repair worn injectors, a failing turbo or a damaged particulate filter. Fix the cause of the smoke and warm the engine fully before the test.

faqs.q: Does an Italian tune-up help before a smoke test?
faqs.a: A hard run gets the engine to full operating temperature, which matters because a cold engine smokes more. It does not fix worn parts that cause high smoke.

faqs.q: What should I do if my truck fails the snap test?
faqs.a: Have a mechanic repair the cause, such as injectors, the turbo, the air intake, exhaust leaks or the particulate filter, then book a retest. Diesel Dynamix explains the result so your shop knows where to start.

faqs.q: Can a truck pass the smoke reading and still fail?
faqs.a: Yes. The smoke test comes with a visual inspection, and missing, disconnected or tampered emissions parts fail the truck even when the smoke reading is fine.

faqs.q: How can an older diesel pass the opacity test?
faqs.a: Warm the engine fully, fix known smoke problems ahead of time, keep the air filter clean and make sure every emissions part is in place and working.

pages.title: Missed Clean Truck Check Deadline? How to Fix It Fast
pages.description: Missed your Clean Truck Check deadline? Learn what non-compliant status means, how DMV holds and penalties work, and how to get back in compliance fast.

sections.heading: What a non-compliant status means
sections.body:
A non-compliant status means CARB's records show the truck is missing at least one requirement. A missed Clean Truck Check deadline is the most common reason, but not the only one.

A truck can be out of compliance if:

- It was not tested before its deadline
- It failed and has not passed a retest
- It is not reported in CTC-VIS
- CARB's annual compliance fee is unpaid

Check the truck in CTC-VIS to see which one applies. Fixing the wrong thing wastes time.

While a truck is non-compliant, a California-registered truck can get a DMV registration hold, which blocks the renewal. Any non-compliant truck that operates can face CARB citations and penalties. CARB sets the amounts, and they can change.

The status does not clear itself. Once the missing step is done, check CTC-VIS again to confirm the truck shows as compliant. If you cannot make sense of what CTC-VIS shows, call us. We help owners with CTC-VIS questions.

sections.heading: Late because the truck failed?
sections.body:
Sometimes a truck is late because it failed and the repair took longer than expected. The path back is the same: repair, retest, confirm.

1. **Get the cause fixed.** Common causes are a check engine light, readiness monitors not set, DPF or emissions faults, and tampered or deleted equipment. Deleted systems fail and are illegal, so the equipment has to be restored.
2. **Let the monitors set.** If codes were cleared or the battery was disconnected during the repair, the truck may need to be driven before an OBD retest.
3. **Book the retest.** We test on site, so the truck does not have to make another trip.
4. **Confirm in CTC-VIS.** Check that the status updates.

To avoid a repeat, test early in the window. That leaves time for a repair if something goes wrong. We give you the next due date after every test and can send reminders. See [fleet testing](/services/fleet-testing) or call **(858) 342-8328**.

faqs.q: Is there a late penalty for Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: A truck that misses its deadline is non-compliant and can face CARB citations and penalties, with amounts set by CARB. California-registered trucks can also get a DMV registration hold.

faqs.q: What does a non-compliant status mean in Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: It means the truck is missing a requirement: a passing test before the deadline, reporting in CTC-VIS or payment of CARB's annual fee. Check CTC-VIS to see which one.

faqs.q: Can a missed Clean Truck Check block my registration?
faqs.a: Yes. The California DMV can hold registration renewal for California-registered vehicles that are not compliant with Clean Truck Check.

faqs.q: How do I fix Clean Truck Check non-compliance?
faqs.a: Find the missing step in CTC-VIS, then report the truck, pay the fee or pass the test as needed. Diesel Dynamix can test on site quickly so the truck gets back in compliance.

faqs.q: Can I still get tested after my Clean Truck Check deadline has passed?
faqs.a: Yes. Get the truck tested as soon as possible, because it stays non-compliant until it passes. Call or WhatsApp (858) 342-8328 to book.

sections.heading: Port of LA Clean Truck Program vs. Clean Truck Check
sections.body:
They are not the same thing. Clean Truck Check is CARB's statewide emissions testing program for heavy-duty vehicles. The port's own Clean Truck Program and its drayage truck registry are separate port rules.

That means a drayage truck can have two sets of requirements:

1. **CARB's Clean Truck Check:** report the truck in CTC-VIS, pay CARB's annual compliance fee there, and pass a test from a tester like us by each deadline.
2. **Port requirements:** whatever the port and its registry ask of trucks entering the terminals. Confirm those with the port directly.

Diesel Dynamix is an independent testing service, not CARB, the port or a government agency. We handle the Clean Truck Check test, explain the result and give you the next due date. We can also help with CTC-VIS questions. For the background on why the state runs this program, see [why California enforces Clean Truck Check](/clean-truck-check/why-california-enforces-it).

sections.heading: Port of LA truck compliance in 2026 and beyond

A bill has proposed cutting testing to once a year, so the schedule may change. Check your own deadlines in CTC-VIS. See our [2026 and 2027 deadline guide](/blog/clean-truck-check-2026-2027-deadlines).

Out-of-state and international drayage trucks that operate in California fall under Clean Truck Check too. We test them near the harbor the same way we test California-plated trucks. More on that in [out-of-state trucks](/blog/clean-truck-check-out-of-state-trucks).

Falling behind has real costs. California-registered trucks can get a DMV registration hold, and CARB can issue citations and penalties. If a drayage truck fails, the usual causes are a check engine light, readiness monitors not set, DPF faults, or tampered or deleted equipment. The truck needs repair and a retest. We do not do repairs, but we tell you exactly what failed.

faqs.a: No. Clean Truck Check is CARB's statewide testing program, while the port's Clean Truck Program is a separate set of port rules. A drayage truck may need to meet both.

faqs.q: Does the port drayage truck registry replace CTC-VIS reporting?
faqs.a: No. Clean Truck Check reporting and compliance fees go through CARB's CTC-VIS system. Confirm any port registry requirements with the port directly.

faqs.q: Can an out-of-state drayage truck get tested near the Port of Los Angeles?
faqs.a: Yes. Out-of-state and international trucks that operate in California need Clean Truck Check, and we test them on site near the harbor.

faqs.a: Yes. Out-of-state and international trucks over 14,000 lb GVWR that operate in California are covered, and they are reported in CTC-VIS the same way as California trucks.

faqs.q: How much is the Clean Truck Check compliance fee?
faqs.a: The amount is set by CARB and shown in CTC-VIS. It is charged per vehicle, once a year. Check CTC-VIS or CARB for the current figure, since CARB can change it.

faqs.q: Is the compliance fee the same as the test cost?
faqs.a: No. The compliance fee is paid to CARB in CTC-VIS once a year per vehicle. The testing fee is charged by your tester each time the truck is tested.

faqs.q: Do I pay the Clean Truck Check fee every year?
faqs.a: Yes. The compliance fee is annual and per vehicle, so plan to pay it every year for each covered vehicle that operates in California.

faqs.q: What happens if the Clean Truck Check fee is not paid?
faqs.a: The truck is not compliant, even with a passing test. California-registered vehicles can get a DMV registration hold, and CARB can issue citations and penalties.

faqs.q: Do out-of-state trucks pay the Clean Truck Check fee?
faqs.a: Yes. Out-of-state and international trucks over 14,000 lb GVWR that operate in California are reported in CTC-VIS and pay the annual compliance fee per vehicle.

faqs.q: Why does the DMV say CARB compliance is required for my truck?
faqs.a: CARB's records show the California-registered truck is not compliant with Clean Truck Check. Common reasons are no passing test on record, a truck not reported in CTC-VIS or an unpaid compliance fee.

faqs.q: How do I remove a CARB hold on my truck registration?
faqs.a: Report the truck in CTC-VIS, pay its annual compliance fee and get a passing test on record. When CTC-VIS shows the truck as compliant, renew with the DMV.

faqs.q: How long after a passed test does the DMV hold clear?
faqs.a: CARB and the DMV control how fast records update, so there is no fixed time we can promise. Check CTC-VIS for the compliant status, and contact CARB if the DMV still shows a hold.

faqs.q: Can a mobile tester clear my DMV hold?
faqs.a: A mobile tester can run and submit the test that makes your truck compliant. The hold itself is released through CARB's and the DMV's systems once the truck shows compliant.

faqs.q: Can I renew registration while the CARB hold is pending?
faqs.a: That is up to the DMV and CARB, so check with them for your situation. The fastest path is usually getting the truck compliant in CTC-VIS right away.

faqs.q: What happens if my truck fails Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: The truck stays non-compliant until it passes. Find out what failed, have it repaired by a qualified shop and retest before your deadline to avoid a DMV hold or CARB penalties.

faqs.q: How soon can I retest after a failed Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: You can book a retest once the repair is done and the truck's readiness monitors have set. CARB sets any rules on retest timing, so check CARB or CTC-VIS for your truck.

faqs.q: Does a failed test get reported to CARB?
faqs.a: Test results are submitted to CARB's system. A truck stays non-compliant until a passing result is on record.

faqs.q: Why did my OBD test get rejected for a VIN mismatch?
faqs.a: The VIN the truck's engine computer reports did not match the VIN on record. Check the VIN in CTC-VIS for typos, and have a repair shop check the engine computer if the record is correct.

faqs.q: What if my truck will not communicate with the OBD tester?
faqs.a: Have a repair shop check the OBD port, wiring, fuses and ECM, and remove any aftermarket devices on the connector. If it still will not communicate, check CARB's rules for your situation.

faqs.q: Will a check engine light fail the Clean Truck Check OBD test?
faqs.a: A check engine light on because of an emissions fault is a common reason trucks fail. Have the fault diagnosed and repaired before the test.

faqs.q: How many readiness monitors can be not ready for Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: CARB sets that rule, and it can depend on the vehicle. Check CARB for your truck, or ask your tester before the test.

faqs.q: How do I set readiness monitors on a diesel truck?
faqs.a: Drive the truck normally after any repair so each monitor can run its self-check. The exact drive cycle varies by engine maker, so ask your dealer or repair shop.

faqs.q: Do pending or permanent codes fail the Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: CARB sets how each code type is treated, so check CARB for your vehicle. Either way, treat them as a sign to get the truck checked before the test.

faqs.q: Should I clear codes before the Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: No. Clearing codes does not fix the problem and resets readiness monitors to not ready, which can cause the truck to fail the OBD test.

faqs.q: Will a deleted truck pass the CARB OBD test?
faqs.a: No. Deleted or tampered emissions systems fail Clean Truck Check, and they are illegal. The truck needs its emissions equipment properly restored and working before it can pass.

faqs.q: Do I need a DPF regen before the Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: If the truck shows a DPF warning or is overdue for regeneration, deal with it before the test, following the engine maker's procedure. A DPF fault with the check engine light on is a common reason for failure.

faqs.q: What causes a diesel to fail the opacity test?
faqs.a: Common causes are worn injectors, a dirty air filter, turbo problems, exhaust leaks, a cracked or plugged DPF and testing with a cold engine. Missing or tampered emissions parts also fail the visual inspection.

faqs.q: What are CARB penalties for emissions deletes?
faqs.a: Tampered and non-compliant trucks face CARB citations and penalties, and California-registered trucks can get a DMV registration hold. CARB sets the penalty amounts, so check CARB for current figures.

faqs.q: Can a reinstalled DPF pass Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: A truck with its emissions equipment properly restored and working can be tested like any other, but it still has to pass on its own. Drive it normally after the repair so readiness monitors can set.

faqs.q: Is Clean Truck Check the same as a smog check?
faqs.a: No. Clean Truck Check is CARB's program for most diesel and alternative-fuel vehicles over 14,000 lb GVWR. California's regular Smog Check is a separate program for lighter vehicles.

faqs.q: Did Clean Truck Check replace PSIP?
faqs.a: Clean Truck Check is CARB's current heavy-duty inspection program and the one that sets today's reporting, fees and test deadlines in CTC-VIS. Check CARB for how older PSIP requirements apply to your fleet.

faqs.q: Can a STAR smog station test a truck over 14,000 lb?
faqs.a: Clean Truck Check tests must be done by a credentialed Clean Truck Check tester. A smog station license is for a different program, so ask any shop whether it performs Clean Truck Check tests.

faqs.q: What is the difference between CARB and BAR testing?
faqs.a: CARB runs Clean Truck Check for most heavy-duty diesel and alternative-fuel vehicles over 14,000 lb GVWR. BAR runs the regular Smog Check program for lighter vehicles.

faqs.q: Is mobile Clean Truck Check testing the same as going to a station?
faqs.a: Yes, it is the same test. A mobile tester comes to your yard, jobsite or terminal, so the truck does not have to be driven to a shop.

faqs.q: Does Clean Truck Check replace a DOT or BIT inspection?
faqs.a: No. Clean Truck Check is an emissions program, while DOT and BIT inspections are safety programs. Passing one does not satisfy the other.

faqs.q: Does my box truck need Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: If your box truck runs on diesel or an alternative fuel and is rated over 14,000 lb GVWR, it most likely needs Clean Truck Check. Check the GVWR on the driver's door label, since smaller box trucks can fall under the line.

faqs.q: Do dump trucks and tow trucks need the test?
faqs.a: Yes, dump trucks and heavy tow trucks over 14,000 lb GVWR that operate in California are covered. Lighter tow trucks on smaller chassis may be under the threshold, so the door label decides.

faqs.q: Do buses and school buses need Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: School buses, transit buses and coach buses over 14,000 lb GVWR are part of the program. Smaller shuttle buses built on light chassis may be under the weight line.

faqs.q: Does an Isuzu NPR or Ford F-550 need it?
faqs.a: It depends on the GVWR of your specific truck. If the door label shows more than 14,000 lb and the engine is diesel or alternative fuel, it needs Clean Truck Check; if it is 14,000 lb or less, it is not covered.

faqs.q: Are agricultural trucks exempt from Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: Agricultural trucks over 14,000 lb are not automatically exempt and are included where they fall under the program. CARB has specific rules for some farm vehicles, so check CARB's rules or CTC-VIS for your truck.

faqs.q: Which test does my vehicle need?
faqs.a: 2013 and newer diesel engines and 2018 and newer alternative-fuel engines get a CARB-verified OBD test. 2012 and older diesels without OBD get a smoke opacity test plus visual inspection, and 2017 and older alternative-fuel engines without OBD get a visual inspection.

faqs.q: Does a one-ton diesel pickup need Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: Most one-ton diesel pickups, like the F-350, Ram 3500 and Silverado 3500, are rated under 14,000 lb GVWR, so they are not covered. Check the GVWR on your own door label to be sure.

faqs.q: Where do I find the GVWR on my truck?
faqs.a: The GVWR is printed on the label on the driver's door or door jamb. Use GVWR, not GCWR, because Clean Truck Check is based on the vehicle's own weight rating.

faqs.q: Do hotshot F-450s and F-550s need Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: Some do. If your F-450 or F-550 is rated over 14,000 lb GVWR and runs on diesel or an alternative fuel, it is likely covered; if it is 14,000 lb or less, it is not.

faqs.q: Is a 3/4-ton diesel under the Clean Truck Check threshold?
faqs.a: Yes. 3/4-ton diesels like the F-250, Ram 2500 and Silverado 2500 are rated well below 14,000 lb GVWR, so they are not part of Clean Truck Check.

faqs.q: Smog check or Clean Truck Check for my diesel pickup?
faqs.a: Clean Truck Check only applies to vehicles over 14,000 lb GVWR, so most diesel pickups are outside it. Whether your pickup needs a regular smog check is a separate DMV question.

faqs.q: Does towing a heavy trailer put my pickup in Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: No. Clean Truck Check is based on the GVWR rating on the door label, not on what you load or tow. Check CARB's rules if your truck has been re-rated or modified.

faqs.q: Does my diesel motorhome need Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: If your motorhome runs on diesel or an alternative fuel, is rated over 14,000 lb GVWR and operates in California, it may be covered. Check CARB's rules or CTC-VIS to confirm for your specific RV.

faqs.q: Are RVs exempt from Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: There is no blanket RV exemption just because a vehicle is a motorhome. CARB's rules decide whether a specific RV is covered, so check CARB or CTC-VIS for yours.

faqs.q: Can the test be done at an RV park or storage lot?
faqs.a: A mobile tester can test the motorhome where it is parked, such as at your home. If it is at a storage lot or RV park, ask about that location when you book.

faqs.q: Do out-of-state motorhomes need Clean Truck Check in California?
faqs.a: Covered vehicles that operate in California are part of the program no matter where they are registered. Check CARB's rules and CTC-VIS for your motorhome.

faqs.q: OBD test or smoke test for my motorhome?
faqs.a: A 2013 or newer diesel engine gets a CARB-verified OBD test. A 2012 or older diesel without OBD gets a smoke opacity test plus a visual inspection.

faqs.q: Where is the OBD port on a Freightliner Cascadia?
faqs.a: Port location varies by model and year, and the tester locates and connects to it during the test. Tell us your make, model and year when you book so we arrive ready.

faqs.q: Does a 9-pin or 16-pin connector matter for the CARB test?
faqs.a: Connector type varies between older and newer trucks, but the test itself is the same CARB-verified OBD test for 2013 and newer diesel engines. Share your truck details when you book so we bring what your truck needs.

faqs.q: Why are my Kenworth readiness monitors not ready?
faqs.a: Clearing codes or disconnecting the battery can leave readiness monitors not set until the truck has been driven normally again. Monitors not set is a common reason OBD tests fail on any brand; ask your mechanic about the right drive cycle.

faqs.q: Do Cummins ISX and Detroit DD15 trucks test the same way?
faqs.a: Yes. Any diesel engine 2013 or newer gets the same CARB-verified OBD test, whatever the engine maker.

faqs.q: Which model years need the OBD test instead of a smoke test?
faqs.a: Diesel engines 2013 and newer, and alternative-fuel engines 2018 and newer, get the OBD test. Diesel engines 2012 and older without OBD get a smoke opacity test plus visual inspection.

faqs.q: Does the truck brand affect Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: No. CARB sets the test by engine type and model year, so Freightliner, Peterbilt, Kenworth, International, Volvo and Mack trucks of the same engine year get the same test.

faqs.q: ¿Qué es el Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: Es el programa de CARB que exige pruebas de emisiones periódicas a la mayoría de los vehículos diésel y de combustible alternativo de más de 14,000 libras GVWR que circulan en California. No es lo mismo que el smog check de los carros.

faqs.q: ¿Cuánto cuesta la prueba de emisiones para camiones?
faqs.a: Hay dos costos: la cuota anual de CARB por vehículo, que se paga en CTC-VIS, y el costo de la prueba que cobra el técnico. Nuestro precio depende de cuántos camiones son, del tipo de prueba y de la ubicación; pida cotización al (858) 342-8328.

faqs.q: ¿Cada cuánto tengo que hacer la prueba?
faqs.a: Hoy la mayoría de los vehículos cubiertos hacen la prueba dos veces al año. Según la regla original de CARB, los vehículos con OBD pasarían a cuatro pruebas al año desde el 1 de octubre de 2027, pero eso puede cambiar; revise su fecha en CTC-VIS.

faqs.q: ¿Cómo registro mi camión en CTC-VIS?
faqs.a: El dueño registra cada camión en CTC-VIS, el sistema de CARB, donde también paga la cuota anual y ve sus fechas límite. Diesel Dynamix le puede ayudar con sus preguntas sobre CTC-VIS.

faqs.q: ¿Aplica a camiones de otro estado o de México?
faqs.a: Sí. El Clean Truck Check cubre a los camiones de más de 14,000 libras GVWR que circulan en California, sin importar si están registrados en otro estado o en México.

faqs.q: ¿Pueden venir a mi yarda?
faqs.a: Sí. Diesel Dynamix hace la prueba en su yarda, obra, terminal, puerto o casa en el sur de California, así que no tiene que manejar a un centro de pruebas.

faqs.q: When is my Clean Truck Check due in 2026?
faqs.a: Each vehicle has its own deadline, shown in CARB's CTC-VIS system. Log in and look up the vehicle by VIN to see its next compliance deadline.

faqs.q: When does Clean Truck Check quarterly testing start?
faqs.a: Under CARB's original rule, OBD-equipped vehicles move to four tests a year starting October 1, 2027. A bill has proposed cutting testing to once a year, so this may change.

faqs.q: Is my Clean Truck Check deadline tied to my DMV registration month?
faqs.a: CARB sets how deadlines are assigned, and the details can depend on the vehicle. Check the deadline shown for your vehicle in CTC-VIS or CARB's rules rather than guessing.

faqs.q: How early can I test before my Clean Truck Check deadline?
faqs.a: CARB decides when a test counts toward a deadline. Check the testing window for your vehicle in CTC-VIS or CARB's rules before booking far ahead.

faqs.q: What changed in Clean Truck Check this year?
faqs.a: Most covered vehicles still test twice a year, with quarterly testing for OBD vehicles scheduled from October 1, 2027 under the original rule. A bill has proposed once-a-year testing, so watch CARB updates and CTC-VIS.

faqs.q: Which vehicles are exempt from Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: Vehicles rated 14,000 lb GVWR or less are outside the program. Other exemptions are set by CARB and depend on the vehicle, so confirm your truck's status in CTC-VIS or CARB's rules before skipping a test.

faqs.q: How long are new trucks exempt from Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: CARB sets whether new vehicles get a delay and when the first test is due. Look up your truck in CTC-VIS for its first deadline rather than assuming it has none.

faqs.q: Do electric trucks still have to register in CTC-VIS?
faqs.a: CARB decides what reporting applies to zero-emission trucks. Check CARB's rules or CTC-VIS for your vehicle.

faqs.q: Is my farm truck exempt from Clean Truck Check?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Agricultural trucks over 14,000 lb are included where they fall under the program, and CARB has specific rules for some farm vehicles, so check CARB's rules for yours.

faqs.q: What if my truck is on non-operational (PNO) status?
faqs.a: CARB sets how non-operational vehicles are handled. Check CARB's rules and keep the vehicle's information current in CTC-VIS.

faqs.q: Can Diesel Dynamix tell me if my truck is exempt?
faqs.a: No. Diesel Dynamix is an independent tester, not CARB, and exemptions are CARB's decision. We can help you read what CTC-VIS shows and test the truck if it is covered.
